exportMeta.featuredStateNote: Featured homepage placement is not stored on portfolio rows; editorial slugs are defined in src/lib/portfolio/home-featured.ts (HOME_FEATURED_SLUGS).
exportMeta.timestampSerializationNote: All exported DateTime columns use PostgreSQL `timestamp without time zone`. Values are serialized as ISO-8601 UTC (Z suffix) using the literal stored wall-clock digits from the database, without applying client-local timezone offsets. Tools that parse naive timestamps as local time (e.g. node-pg Date.toISOString() on a PDT host) may display a +7h shift; that is a read-path artifact, not the stored value.

The site presents business information, FAQs, events, customer reviews, contact details, and social links through a mobile-friendly experience designed around the client's existing brand.
caseStudies.problem: The Royal Canine needed a dedicated web presence that could communicate how its self-service dog wash works, answer common customer questions, promote events, display business information and reviews, and give customers straightforward ways to contact or follow the business. The experience also needed to reflect the client's existing visual identity and work effectively on mobile devices.
caseStudies.solution: I built a multi-page React website around the client's business content and branding. The site combines business information, FAQs, events, customer reviews, contact details, imagery, and social links with responsive navigation and interactive elements such as image carousels and modals. The implementation was refined through multiple rounds of client feedback before delivery.
caseStudies.architecture: The application was built with React, TypeScript, and Vite using React Router for page navigation and CSS Modules for component-level styling. Business and event content was separated into reusable data structures, while shared components handled navigation, imagery, carousels, modals, and recurring presentation patterns across the site.
caseStudies.challenges: Much of the development involved turning an existing business identity and client-provided content into a consistent responsive experience. Navigation, hero imagery, carousels, modals, FAQs, event cards, contact elements, and page layouts required repeated refinement across different screen sizes. Client feedback also resulted in frequent adjustments to wording, imagery, spacing, colors, links, and component behavior throughout development.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: This project gave me early experience working through a structured code-review process rather than developing entirely in isolation. My implementation branches were reviewed before being merged, and feedback often required additional debugging, refinement, or changes before approval. Working through that review cycle helped strengthen my development practices and taught me to see feedback and iteration as part of producing quality software, not simply as corrections after the work was finished.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: The application was delivered to the client for continued ownership and maintenance. Later repository activity shows ongoing dependency and content maintenance after handoff, while future modernization could include further accessibility, performance, SEO, and component-system improvements.

caseStudies.caption: Ghost Mammoth Pickleball
caseStudies.description: A production pickleball platform built around live event operations, with player registration, real-time queues and court assignments, membership billing, and administrative event management.
caseStudies.keyFeatures: Event registration • Player skill levels • Real-time player queue • Court assignments • Match notifications • Group registration • Event administration • Court management • Stripe subscriptions • Membership access • Real-time synchronization
caseStudies.role: Full-stack contributor working collaboratively on product architecture, event workflows, authentication and authorization, subscription billing, realtime functionality, administrative features, frontend implementation, testing, and production refinement.
caseStudies.highlights: Next.js • TypeScript • Supabase • PostgreSQL • Supabase Realtime • Stripe • Row Level Security • Vercel
caseStudies.subtitle: Real-time event and court management for pickleball communities
caseStudies.summary: A production membership and event management platform for a pickleball community, combining event registration, skill-based player queues, real-time court assignments, group participation, subscription billing, and administrative event operations.
caseStudies.problem:
A real-time domain system that continuously determines who plays next, how groups remain together, which players fit available courts, how winners rotate, and how those decisions remain synchronized between administrators and participants.


Pickleball events require more coordination than simply allowing players to register. Organizers need to manage participants with different skill levels, maintain a fair player queue, assign players to available courts, communicate changes in real time, and manage membership access without forcing staff to manually coordinate every transition during an active event.
caseStudies.solution: We built Ghost Mammoth as a production membership and event-management platform centered around the live event workflow. Players can join events, provide their skill level, enter the playing queue, and receive court assignments and updates as an event progresses. Administrators can create and manage events, configure courts, oversee player rotation, generate matchups, and end sessions while membership access is handled through subscription billing.
caseStudies.architecture: The application uses Next.js and TypeScript for the application layer with Supabase providing PostgreSQL persistence, authentication, and realtime infrastructure. Supabase Realtime synchronizes event and court state between participants and administrators, while Stripe handles subscription checkout and membership billing. Row Level Security provides database-level access controls alongside application authorization.
caseStudies.challenges: The core challenge was coordinating state that changes continuously during a live event. Queue position, court availability, player assignments, event state, and administrative actions can affect multiple users simultaneously. The system therefore had to keep participant and administrator views synchronized while maintaining predictable queue and assignment behavior.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Real-time applications require thinking differently about state than conventional request-and-response CRUD systems. Changes made by one participant or administrator can immediately affect several other users, making synchronization, authorization, failure handling, and clearly defined ownership of business logic especially important. The project also reinforced the value of dividing complex domain logic into reusable modules and shared contracts as the system grows.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: Continued development can expand group registration workflows, improve captain and team-management capabilities, refine event rotation and matchmaking behavior, strengthen administrative analytics, and continue improving the participant experience during live events.

caseStudies.caption: Tournament Registration & Event Management System
caseStudies.description: A reusable tournament registration and event management system built around the organizers' actual workflow, including player signup, payment verification, team management, waitlisting, administrative tools, and support for future annual events.
caseStudies.keyFeatures: Player registration • Skill-level collection • Preferred-player requests • Waitlist management • Payment proof uploads • Payment verification • Team organization • Administrative player management • CSV export • Reusable annual event workflow
caseStudies.role: Sole developer responsible for requirements discovery, workflow design, application architecture, database design, frontend and backend development, security controls, deployment, and continued feature development.
caseStudies.highlights: Next.js • TypeScript • PostgreSQL • Neon • Server Actions • Authentication • File uploads • Rate limiting • Responsive UI
caseStudies.subtitle: From tournament registration site to reusable event operations platform
caseStudies.summary: A production registration and event operations platform built for an annual golf tournament, handling player signup, payment verification, team organization, administrative corrections, waitlisting, and reusable workflows for future events.
caseStudies.problem: The tournament organizers needed a simpler way to manage player registration for an annual golf event. Registration involved collecting individual player information, skill levels, preferred teammates, payment confirmation, and eventually organizing players into foursomes. Manual coordination made it easy for names to be entered incorrectly, registrations to require intervention, and tournament data to become difficult to manage as the event approached.
caseStudies.solution: I initially built the system around the tournament's immediate registration needs: collecting individual player information, skill levels, preferred teammates, and payment proof while giving organizers an administrative workflow for reviewing registrations. Once the system was in use, additional operational needs emerged. I expanded the administration tools so organizers could correct player information, manually manage registrations, organize teams, handle exceptions, and preserve the system for future tournaments rather than rebuilding it each year.
caseStudies.architecture: The application uses Next.js and TypeScript with PostgreSQL hosted on Neon for persistent tournament and registration data. Public registration workflows are separated from authenticated administrative functionality. Server-side validation, rate limiting, restricted administrative access, controlled file handling, and defensive CSV export behavior protect registration data while keeping the public signup process straightforward. The application was developed incrementally through planned phases, keeping public registration, domain logic, storage, and administrative workflows separated as the system expanded.
caseStudies.challenges: The biggest challenge came after the initial registration workflow was working. Real-world use exposed cases that weren't as important during the original build: players could enter information incorrectly, some needed help completing registration, organizers needed more direct control over player records, and the application needed to support future tournaments. Those requirements had to be added without disrupting the live registration workflow or compromising existing data.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Production use revealed requirements that weren't obvious during the initial build. The public registration flow handled the expected path, but the administrative tools had to handle everything that happened when users didn't follow that path. This reinforced the importance of designing business software for exception handling and operator intervention, while keeping the architecture flexible enough to accommodate workflows that emerge after launch.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: Future development can continue improving multi-event support, historical tournament archiving, event configuration, team organization, and administrative reporting as the organizers reuse the platform for future tournaments.

caseStudies.keyFeatures: Lead and client management • Project management • Quotes and proposals • Contract workflows • Invoice management • Stripe payment integration • Financial tracking • Business expense management • Business development tracking • Upwork job evaluation and proposal tracking • Work logging • Weekly business reporting • PDF report generation • Project membership and authorization • Client-facing token workflows • Reusable design system • Storybook component documentation • Configuration-driven UI architecture
caseStudies.role: Sole architect and developer responsible for product planning, business workflow analysis, system architecture, database design, backend development, frontend implementation, security, testing, deployment, documentation, and continuous platform evolution.
caseStudies.highlights: Next.js 16 • React 19 • TypeScript • Prisma • Neon PostgreSQL • Auth.js v5 • Stripe • Storybook • Playwright • Zod • CSS Modules • Server Components • Server Actions
caseStudies.subtitle: From internal business tool to a scalable operations platform
caseStudies.summary: A custom business operations platform built to manage the full DevLaunch Systems workflow, from leads and proposals through clients, projects, contracts, invoicing, financial tracking, business development, and reporting. The CRM has evolved through multiple development phases as real business needs exposed new workflows, architectural requirements, and opportunities for automation.
caseStudies.problem: DevLaunch Systems initially needed a better way to manage basic business administration such as leads, clients, projects, quotes, contracts, and invoices. Using disconnected documents and external tools would have fragmented information across multiple systems and made it harder to connect business development, project delivery, finances, and reporting. As the business began operating, new requirements continued to emerge from the actual workflows being used day to day.
caseStudies.solution: I built a custom CRM around the business process rather than starting with a fixed feature list. The system began with core business administration and evolved incrementally as new workflows became necessary. Leads could become clients and projects, quotes could progress into contracts and invoices, payments and expenses could feed financial records, and later versions expanded into project management, business development, work tracking, analytics, reporting, and reusable engineering infrastructure. This allowed the platform to grow alongside the business instead of requiring a complete rebuild whenever the workflow changed.
caseStudies.architecture: The CRM uses a layered Next.js architecture with React Server Components and server-side workflows backed by Prisma and Neon PostgreSQL. Business entities are modeled around the relationships between leads, clients, projects, quotes, contracts, invoices, payments, expenses, users, and project memberships. Auth.js provides authentication while application and database authorization controls protect administrative and project-scoped operations. Stripe integrations are handled through persisted application state and webhook-driven workflows. Later development phases introduced reusable UI primitives, centralized design tokens, Storybook documentation, configuration-driven interfaces, stronger testing boundaries, and architectural standards intended to support future developers and continued platform growth.
caseStudies.challenges: The largest challenge has been evolving a production system while actively using it to run the business. Requirements were not known upfront because many became visible only after the underlying workflow was used in practice. New capabilities therefore had to coexist with existing data and workflows without destabilizing working features. As the CRM grew, another challenge emerged: functionality was increasing faster than the application's original organization could comfortably support, requiring deliberate codebase restructuring, stronger architectural boundaries, reusable UI patterns, security hardening, and better documentation.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Building around stable business concepts while allowing workflows to evolve has been more valuable than trying to predict every future requirement. The project reinforced the importance of separating business logic from presentation, keeping authorization close to protected resources, using incremental migrations instead of large rewrites, and documenting architectural decisions before knowledge becomes dependent on one developer. It also demonstrated that internal software can become an engineering platform over time when repeated workflows are turned into reusable systems instead of isolated features.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: Planned development continues the transition from a founder-built internal application toward a system another developer could safely understand and extend. Current work includes configuration-driven navigation and metadata, reusable form and DataTable patterns, standardized feedback components, stronger developer onboarding, continued authorization and security improvements, AI-assisted business workflows, and further automation between business development, project management, reporting, and engineering processes.

caseStudies.description: A custom-built engineering portfolio platform that evolved over multiple years from a static website into a full portfolio management system. The platform now includes a structured admin interface, media management, engineering case studies, project metrics, version timelines, SEO management, and reusable content workflows without requiring source code changes for day-to-day updates.
caseStudies.keyFeatures: Engineering case studies • Cloudflare R2 media library • Project evolution timelines • SEO management • Media picker • Version history •  Project metrics • Authentication & authorization
caseStudies.role: Sole architect and developer responsible for product planning, UX, database design, backend architecture, frontend implementation, deployment, and continuous evolution.
caseStudies.highlights: Next.js 16 • React 19 • TypeScript • Prisma • Neon PostgreSQL • Cloudflare R2 • Auth.js • Server Actions • Zod • CSS Modules
caseStudies.subtitle: From static website to a production engineering platform
caseStudies.summary: A production portfolio management platform designed to showcase engineering work through structured case studies, media management, project evolution, technical documentation, SEO management, and reusable administrative workflows.
caseStudies.problem: My original portfolio was a traditional developer website where every content update required changing source code. Updating project information, replacing images, creating case studies, or adding SEO metadata all required editing files, rebuilding the application, and redeploying. As the number of projects, articles, and engineering content grew, maintaining the portfolio became increasingly inefficient.
caseStudies.solution: Instead of rebuilding from scratch, I evolved the portfolio into a dedicated engineering platform. I designed a structured administration system that separates engineering content from application code while introducing media management, project documentation, reusable workflows, and database-driven content management. The result allows nearly all portfolio updates to occur through the admin interface rather than source code.
caseStudies.architecture: The application follows a layered architecture separating presentation, business logic, persistence, and infrastructure. Next.js Server Components handle rendering, Prisma manages data access, Neon PostgreSQL stores structured project content, Cloudflare R2 provides object storage, and reusable service layers isolate storage, validation, and business rules. The storage implementation uses an abstract provider interface so local storage and S3-compatible services can be swapped without application changes.
caseStudies.challenges: The largest engineering challenge was evolving an existing production application without breaking current functionality. Every new capability—including media management, project timelines, engineering stories, metrics, authentication improvements, and SEO fields—had to coexist with legacy data while remaining backward compatible throughout the migration.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned: Building systems incrementally is often more valuable than rewriting them. Careful planning, layered abstractions, backward compatibility, and phased migrations allowed the platform to continue functioning while its architecture evolved significantly underneath. The project reinforced the importance of designing systems that support future workflows instead of only today's requirements.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: Planned enhancements include AI-assisted content generation, project analytics, automated image optimization, MDX documentation support, version comparison, reusable design-system documentation, and tighter integration with the internal CRM and engineering workflow platform.

caseStudies.caption: IntelliTaskPro
caseStudies.description: A multi-tenant project management SaaS built around real team workflows, with Kanban boards, RBAC, AI-assisted task planning, Stripe billing, real-time updates, recurring tasks, automation, and external integrations.
caseStudies.keyFeatures: Multi-tenant organizations • Kanban project boards • Task and sprint management • Role-based access control • AI-assisted task and sprint generation • Real-time collaboration • Recurring tasks Automation workflows • Stripe subscriptions and billing • Usage tracking • GitHub synchronization • External integrations • Notifications Audit logging • Full-text search • Accessibility and E2E testing
caseStudies.role: Sole product architect and primary developer responsible for product design, application architecture, database modeling, multi-tenant authorization, billing, AI integration, workflow automation, integrations, testing, deployment, and continued platform evolution.
caseStudies.highlights: Next.js • React • TypeScript • Prisma • Neon PostgreSQL • Stripe • Redis • BullMQ • Pusher • AI provider abstraction • Playwright • Tailwind CSS
caseStudies.subtitle: Multi-tenant project management and collaboration SaaS
caseStudies.summary: A full-stack SaaS platform for managing projects, teams, tasks, sprints, recurring work, integrations, and subscription billing. IntelliTaskPro combines multi-tenant architecture, role-based permissions, real-time collaboration, AI-assisted workflows, automation, and external integrations within a production-oriented project management system.
caseStudies.problem: Project management applications often treat tasks as isolated CRUD records, while actual team workflows involve permissions, project context, recurring work, notifications, billing, integrations, automation, and collaboration. I wanted to build a system around those relationships rather than simply creating another task board.
caseStudies.solution: I developed IntelliTaskPro as a multi-tenant SaaS platform where organizations can manage projects, boards, tasks, sprints, recurring work, and team access from one system. The platform combines project management with real-time updates, AI-assisted planning, subscription billing, automation, notifications, and integrations while maintaining clear tenant and permission boundaries.
caseStudies.architecture:
IntelliTaskPro uses a Next.js and TypeScript application architecture backed by PostgreSQL through Prisma. Organizations provide the tenant boundary, with role and permission checks controlling access to application resources. Business capabilities such as billing, AI providers, integrations, notifications, automation, and data access are separated into dedicated services rather than being embedded directly into UI components.

External systems including Stripe, GitHub, Slack, Jira, Linear, Zapier, Pusher, and AI providers are handled through integration or abstraction layers so application workflows are not tightly coupled to individual providers.
caseStudies.challenges:
The largest challenge has been managing the interactions between features as the platform expanded. Adding organizations, permissions, billing, recurring tasks, AI workflows, real-time updates, and integrations meant that individual features could no longer be designed in isolation.

Changes increasingly had to account for tenant boundaries, authorization, subscription state, asynchronous work, external services, and existing workflows. This pushed the architecture toward clearer service boundaries and reusable domain logic.
caseStudies.lessonsLearned:
Building IntelliTaskPro reinforced that SaaS complexity comes less from individual features than from the relationships between them. A task may involve permissions, billing limits, notifications, automation, synchronization, and real-time state at the same time.

The project also reinforced the value of provider abstractions and separating business logic from presentation code. Those boundaries make it much easier to evolve a system without rewriting unrelated functionality.
caseStudies.futureImprovements: Continue strengthening the platform architecture, expand automation capabilities, improve integration workflows, increase observability, extend AI-assisted project workflows, and continue refining the application around real team usage.
